subject: Maths
title: Solving by substitution
subtitle: Simultaneous Equations · GCSE Maths
learning_objective: I can solve simultaneous linear equations by substituting one equation into the other.

key_vocab.definition: The substitution method involves rearranging one equation to make a variable the subject, then replacing that variable in the other equation.

sections.title: Learning Objective
sections.content: I can solve simultaneous linear equations by substituting one equation into the other.

sections.title: Key Words
sections.content: substitution method -- The substitution method involves rearranging one equation to make a variable the subject, then replacing that variable in the other equation.

sections.title: Method
sections.content:
Make one variable the subject of one equation, then substitute that expression into the other equation.
y = 3x − 1; 2x + y = 9 ⇒ 2x + 3x − 1 = 9
Replace y with the expression from the first equation

Key examples:
  ✓ y = 2x + 1 into 3x + y = 11: 3x + (2x+1) = 11  (direct substitution)
  ✓ x = 5 − y into 2x + 3y = 13: 2(5−y) + 3y = 13  (rearrange first)
  ✓ Best when one variable already has coefficient 1  (easy to rearrange)
  ✗ y = 2x + 1 into 3x + y = 11 gives 3x + 2x + 1 = 11 but answer is x = 3  (5x + 1 = 11, x = 2)
  ✗ Substitution cannot be used for linear equations  (it works for any system)

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
Example 1 – y already the subject
  Solve y = 2x + 1 and 3x + y = 11
  Substitute y = 2x + 1 into equation 2: 3x + (2x + 1) = 11
  5x + 1 = 11 ⇒ 5x = 10 ⇒ x = 2
  y = 2(2) + 1 = 5
  x = 2, y = 5
  (When y is already isolated, substitute directly.)

Example 2 – rearrange first
  Solve x + y = 8 and 2x + 3y = 21
  From eq 1: y = 8 − x
  Substitute: 2x + 3(8 − x) = 21 ⇒ 2x + 24 − 3x = 21
  −x = −3, so x = 3; y = 8 − 3 = 5
  x = 3, y = 5
  (Rearrange the simpler equation to make y the subject.)

sections.title: y is already the subject
sections.content:
Solve by substitution.

(a) y = x + 3 and 2x + y = 12
(b) y = 3x and x + y = 8
(c) y = 2x − 1 and x + y = 8
(d) y = x + 5 and 3x + y = 13

sections.title: Rearrange one equation
sections.content:
Rearrange, then substitute.

(a) x + y = 10 and 3x + 2y = 26
(b) x + y = 7 and 2x + 5y = 20
(c) x + 2y = 9 and 3x + y = 12
(d) x − y = 1 and 3x + 2y = 18

sections.title: x as the subject
sections.content:
Make x the subject, then substitute.

(a) x = 2y and 3x + y = 14
(b) x = y + 4 and 2x + 3y = 18
(c) x = 3y − 1 and x + 2y = 9
(d) x = 10 − 2y and 3x + y = 15

sections.title: More complex
sections.content:
Solve by substitution.

(a) 2y = x + 3 and 3x + 4y = 21
(b) x = 2y − 5 and 4x + 3y = 9
(c) y = 3x − 7 and 2x + y = 3
(d) x + 3y = 11 and 2x − y = 1

sections.title: Mixed substitution
sections.content:
Solve using substitution.

(a) y = 4x − 3 and 2x + y = 9
(b) x + y = 5 and 3x − 2y = 5
(c) y = x − 4 and 5x + 2y = 27
(d) 2x + y = 11 and x − y = 1
(e) x = 2y − 3 and 3x + 4y = 21

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
✓ Substitution works by replacing a variable with an equivalent expression
✗ You must always make y the subject
✓ After solving for one variable, substitute back to find the other
✗ Substitution only works when y is already the subject
✓ You should always check your answer in both original equations

  (c) x = 2, y = −1
